rows.text: This looks straightforward enough to get into — labeled fields, a disabled-until-valid button, live password hints, Enter-to-submit. The CRO branching ("On behalf of clients") is exactly the framing my team lives in, so I'd know immediately which path to take. Nothing here would trip up a medium-comfort user on my team.

Honestly this looks straightforward to get into — labeled fields, a disabled button until things are filled, Enter-to-submit, and the MFA step is exactly what I'd expect. The CRO fork ("On behalf of clients") is a nice touch since that's how my team actually works, and the live password helper removes the guessing. Nothing here would slow down a regulatory associate.

The three-column layout with a numbered journey rail, a "You're here" marker, and locked steps with plain-language reasons is genuinely how my juniors would want to work, so the guided path looks approachable. What I can't tell from a walkthrough is how it holds up when a real filing goes sideways mid-sequence, and ten steps is a lot to keep gated cleanly. The Expert mode toggle is a smart concession for people like me who don't want to be blocked.

The three-column layout with a numbered journey rail, active step card, and readiness panel is the kind of structure my team could follow without much hand-holding, and the locked-steps-with-reasons approach mirrors how we actually gate work. What I can't judge from a walkthrough is how it holds up when a real filing goes sideways — resubmissions, deficiency responses, mid-sequence changes — because a clean 10-step happy path is easy to draw and hard to live in.

This looks manageable for me and my team — the New dossier form maps cleanly onto how we already think about a product file, and the ID validation catching the one-letter-plus-6-or-7-digits pattern up front would save us the back-and-forth we get in Vault. The placeholder-ID path is a sensible touch since REP-issued Dossier IDs never arrive on our schedule. My only friction is the sheer number of nav destinations (Journey, Dossiers, Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence) with no explanation here of how they differ.

This reads as fairly intuitive for anyone who's touched a RIM system. Creating a dossier, filtering, grid versus list, the archive workflow with a typed-ID confirmation — none of that would trip up my team. The typed-ID-plus-reason gate before archiving is a small friction, but it's the right kind of friction, so I don't mind it.

The three-column layout is familiar enough to anyone coming from Vault or docuBridge, so my team would orient quickly. But there is a lot on screen at once, and the reliance on nested expanders and hover tooltips for critical information worries me for a mixed-skill team of nine who file under deadline pressure. I would want to see it hands-on before judging whether the density helps or overwhelms.

Honestly, this looks dense — three columns, nested expanders inside expanders, mode toggles inside forms. My team lives in Vault and docuBridge, so a section tree with status icons is familiar territory, but I'd want to see how much clicking it takes to actually place one leaf. The AI-vs-form toggle and the "review vs Health Canada" step add cognitive load, though the pre-filled known facts and drop zones would genuinely speed us up once we're past the learning curve.

If the layout is as described, I could find my way around it — the Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A choice maps to how we actually triage sections. But there's a lot stacked in one panel: eyebrow, guidance box, two disclosures, an accountability note, then the chat, then two separate confirmation steps. I'd want to see whether my junior associates get lost in it, because in Vault my team already knows where things live and this is a new mental model.

The panel itself looks manageable — Upload, author, or mark N/A is a familiar pattern, and a chat box with a Send button is not going to intimidate anyone on my team. My worry is the sheer number of states and expanders — Format & source, eCTD placement, "More on how the AI is kept accountable," two sub-toggles under Author in-app — that's a lot of nesting to teach nine people consistently. Once you know the path it's fine, but the first pass would need a written SOP.

Assuming the module pages are already filled, this looks straightforward to operate — the findings list, the collapsed expanders, and the export chip are all familiar patterns from Vault and docuBridge. What I can't judge from a walkthrough is how much manual leaf placement sits upstream of this screen; if my team has to hand-place every document before the check runs, "easy" evaporates fast.

The layout is dense but it follows the mental model I already carry from Vault and docuBridge, so my senior people would find their footing quickly. The collapsed-by-default expanders keep the initial view manageable, which I appreciate. My worry is the junior analysts on my team drowning in chips and toggles the first time through, so I'd want a short onboarding pass before I let them near a live sequence.

The layout is dense but it follows the mental model I already carry — portfolio, registry, correspondence, audit are the four buckets my team lives in, so I could find my way. The scope card and the show/hide grid are sensible, and the 30-day deadline card is exactly the kind of thing I currently keep in a fragile Excel tracker. My concern for a mid-comfort team is the sheer number of chips, popovers and expanders on one screen; some of my juniors would need training before they stopped missing things behind the collapsed "Advanced" and "Details" expanders.

The layout is dense but it follows the mental model my team already uses — a portfolio grid, per-dossier drill-down, a registry, correspondence, and audit — so I could navigate it without much hand-holding. I appreciate that the grid and details are progressively disclosed rather than dumping everything at once. My only friction is the sheer number of chips, popovers and expanders per row; my junior associates will need a short orientation before they stop missing things behind the "Details" and "Advanced" collapses.

The three-column layout with a step rail, active card, and a submission tower on the right is a pattern my team would recognize instantly from Vault, so the navigation feels approachable. What reassures me most is that they've kept the destructive actions deliberate — typing "RESET" in a modal, opt-in AI per section — which tells me someone who's been audited designed this. I'd want hands-on time before judging real friction, but on paper this reads as low-effort to pick up.

On paper this looks navigable — a clear top nav, a guided journey rail, a submission tower on the right. But I can't judge ease from a walkthrough; my real test is whether my team of nine can move through a live sequence without me babysitting them. The three-column layout and the readiness chip are the kind of thing that either genuinely reduces cognitive load or becomes clutter, and I'd need hands-on time to know which.

Honestly this looks straightforward to get through — labeled fields, a disabled-until-filled button, Enter-to-submit, MFA code field, the usual. Nothing here would slow me down; it's a standard auth flow with sensible affordances. The CRO-versus-own-company branch and the live password helper are the kind of small touches that reduce fumbling.

This part looks straightforward to me. Sign in, MFA with a 6-digit authenticator code, workspace creation with a CRO-versus-own-company branch, password reset — it's all the standard auth flow I do in my sleep, and the disabled-until-filled button and live password helper are the kind of small touches that keep me from fumbling. Nothing here would slow me down.

The three-column layout with a numbered journey rail, active step card, and readiness column reads like something I could pick up fast, and honestly it looks more approachable than fighting eCTD Office's folder structure. The locked-steps-with-plain-reasons plus an Expert mode toggle is smart — it won't box in someone like me who assembles daily but still guards a first-timer. My only worry is whether ten linear steps hold up when real ANDS work is messy and non-sequential; I bounce between Module 3 and validation constantly.

Honestly this looks manageable for someone like me — the numbered rail with "You're here," locked steps with reasons, and an Expert mode that unblocks navigation is exactly what I'd want so I'm not held hostage by a wizard. The dashed-underline term reveals are a nice touch for juniors, though I personally wouldn't need them. My worry is the ten discrete steps feeling slow when I'm doing 15 sequences a year and already know the drill.

Honestly this reads like it'd be easy for me to pick up — the New dossier form is basically the metadata I already fill in eCTD Office, and the ID validation regex (one letter + 6-7 digits) matches Health Canada's dossier format so I wouldn't fight it. The grid/list toggle, filters, and sortable columns with a "soonest due" and overdue flag are exactly how I triage my 15 sequences a year, so no learning curve there. The placeholder-ID path is a nice touch since we often start assembly before the Dossier ID Request clears REP.

This looks straightforward for someone like me who does assembly daily — creating a dossier is just an ID, product name, and submission type, and the placeholder auto-fill is a nice touch for when you're still waiting on the REP Dossier ID Request. The grid/list toggle, filtering by owner/client, and the sortable table with soonest-due are exactly how I'd triage 15 sequences a year. Nothing here would slow me down.

Honestly, this looks manageable for someone like me who does eCTD assembly daily. The three-column layout with section tree, section detail, and a transmit-readiness panel maps cleanly onto how I already think in eCTD Office. The one thing I'd want to feel out hands-on is how much clicking through collapsed expanders it takes to get to leaf placement and href — I live in that detail all day and I don't want it buried behind three accordions.

Honestly, if the columns behave the way this describes, I could work fast in it — the section tree with required/optional and the M1 badge maps straight onto how I think in eCTD Office, and having the leaf/placement panel right next to the section is better than bouncing between the backbone and my documents. My worry is density: three columns, nested expanders, buckets, toggles — first hour would be a lot of hunting, and I do this daily so I'd want keyboard nav and not a click maze.

The plain-language eCTD primer and the "what HC needs here" box are nice for a junior, but for me they'd be noise I'd want collapsed by default, which it sounds like they are.

Honestly this looks straightforward for someone like me — the three-way Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A split maps to how I already think about each leaf, and the chat box plus "Use this draft" flow is self-explanatory. I appreciate that Enter sends and the states ("Thinking…", "Saving…", "Recording…") tell me what's happening. My only friction is the number of gates you have to click through before a section counts as done, but that's a fair trade.

Honestly this reads as pretty easy for someone like me — pick Upload, Author in-app, or Mark N/A, then chat or fill a form. I do this kind of assembly daily so the toggle model is intuitive. My only friction is that it's a lot of reading before I get to actually produce anything, but that's a one-time cost.

If it works as written, this would be easy for me — I already live in eCTD folder structures and lifecycle operators, so a Files/Outline viewer with per-sequence "new/replace" chips and a purpose-tagged sequence list maps cleanly onto how I actually work. The collapsed-by-default expanders keep the surface clean, and gating export on the completeness check with a fix-or-override path is exactly the workflow I'd expect. My only friction is that a lot is hidden behind toggles, so a new sequence would take me a few clicks to feel confident nothing silently passed.

Honestly this looks well-organized and I'd move through it fast — collapsed ghost buttons, findings capped at 5 errors/3 warnings with a show-all toggle, sequence cards with purpose chips and active badges. That maps closely to how I already work in eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit, so the learning curve is near zero. The one friction point is the override-requires-a-typed-reason gate, but that's the right kind of friction, not annoying friction.

Layout-wise this reads like it'd be easy for me — a portfolio grid with one primary status chip per dossier, scope selectors, and expanders that hide the fee/litigation detail until I want it is exactly how I'd want to triage 15 sequences. The one-chip-per-row discipline is smart; my current SharePoint views are a mess of columns. My only friction is the sheer number of stacked concepts (scope card, summary cards, deadline card, grid toggle) all on the Portfolio page, but nothing here looks hard to learn.

The layout reads like it was built by someone who's actually assembled a sequence — portfolio, registry, correspondence, audit all separated the way I'd expect, and the scope card sitting first is sensible. That said, there's a lot packed into each row with nested expanders, and I'd want to click through it live before saying it's genuinely fast; a written walkthrough always looks tidier than daily use.

If it's as guided as this reads, it'd be easy for me — a step rail, module tower, and readiness chip is basically the mental model I already carry from eCTD Office and GlobalSubmit. My worry is the opposite of hard: over-hand-holding. I assemble ~15 sequences a year and don't want to click through a wizard when I already know the eCTD spec cold; I'd need a way to move fast, not just "step by step."

On paper this reads as very navigable for someone like me — clear top nav, a journey rail, a submission tower, readiness percentage. That's the same mental model as eCTD Office's module tree, so I'd be up and running fast. My worry is always what happens when the guided flow doesn't match a real-world edge case, but the walkthrough doesn't show me that, so I'll call it "looks easy" with a caveat.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable. The disabled-until-filled button, the live password helper counting down characters, and Enter-to-submit are all things I'd expect, so I wouldn't get stuck signing in or making a workspace. The "Who are you filing for?" split into own-company vs CRO is smart since I'm at a CRO, and the demo-code reveal means I wouldn't be locked out fumbling for an email that never arrives.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for me. The fields are labeled plainly, the primary button tells me when it's disabled and shows "Working…", and Enter-to-submit is a nice touch. The CRO path where I pick "On behalf of clients" and the labels change to "Client company name" is exactly my situation, so I wouldn't feel lost setting up.

Honestly this looks manageable for me. The numbered "filing journey" rail with a "You're here" marker and locked later steps means I can't get lost or skip ahead, which is exactly what I need since I've only done this once or twice. The three-column layout is a lot on screen at once, but the guided one-step-at-a-time flow keeps it from being overwhelming.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for someone like me — the numbered journey rail with a "You're here" marker and locked steps that tell you why they're locked would keep me from getting lost, which is exactly what happens to me now with the Word templates. I like that Expert mode is opt-in, so I won't accidentally skip something I shouldn't. My only worry is that ten steps plus three columns of stuff is a lot on screen at once, and I'd need a bit of time before it stopped feeling busy.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for me. The "New dossier +" form is just a handful of fields I recognize, and the placeholder-ID option means I'm not stuck if Health Canada hasn't issued the real Dossier ID yet, which is exactly the situation I keep hitting. The inline validation catching a bad ID format before I submit would save me the embarrassment of a senior having to point it out.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for me. The "New dossier +" form is just a few fields and the placeholder-ID option means I'm not stuck if Health Canada hasn't issued the real Dossier ID yet, which is exactly the situation I'm in right now. The filter bar and "Just my dossiers" checkbox would save me scrolling once we have a few files going.

Honestly it looks like a lot at once — three columns, badges, chips, expanders inside expanders. As someone still learning the eCTD side, I think I'd be clicking around nervously at first, but the fact that everything has hover tooltips and plain-language primers makes me think I could actually find my footing without pinging a senior every five minutes. The "Author in-app" form pre-filling known facts and flagging "example — replace this" fields sounds like it would genuinely save me from silly mistakes.

Honestly this looks like a lot at once. Three columns, badges, chips, expanders inside expanders. I think once someone showed me where the AI draft and upload buttons live I'd be fine, but on my first ANDS I'd probably feel a bit lost and click around nervously. The step-by-step flow (pick section, upload or author, review, confirm) does seem findable though.

Honestly, this looks pretty approachable for me — I'd just type what I know about the submission into a chat box, kind of like typing an email, and it drafts the section. The three big buttons (Upload, Author in-app, Mark N/A) make the choices obvious. My only worry is the number of steps to actually "finish": draft, then "Use this draft", then a whole separate "I have reviewed this — it is my content" attestation before it counts. That's a lot of clicking but I get why it's there.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable — the three big buttons (Upload, Author in-app, Mark N/A) tell me exactly where to start, and typing a plain sentence about the sponsor into a chat box is something I can do without training. My one worry is the sheer number of expanders and disclosures stacked on the screen (Format & source, eCTD placement, "More on how the AI is kept accountable"); as someone still learning the terminology I'd probably click into all of them nervously to make sure I'm not missing something.

Honestly it looks like a lot of buttons and expanders, but most of them are collapsed by default so I think I could find my way around without panicking. The "Show all N findings" and the plain-language error messages would help me a lot, since right now I chase this stuff manually in Word. I'd probably need a senior to walk me through it once, but after that it seems manageable.

Honestly the layout sounds manageable, everything is broken into cards and collapsible sections so I wouldn't be overwhelmed on day one. But there's a LOT packed in here — rule catalogues, parity-gap tables, lifecycle operators, sequences with override reasons — and as someone still learning the terminology I'd be clicking into every expander just to figure out what I'm looking at. I'd probably need a senior to walk me through my first export.

Honestly this feels dense for someone at my level — there's a lot packed onto each page (scope cards, chips, expanders, mini module towers) and I'd need someone to walk me through it once. That said, the layout sounds logical, and things like the 30-day deadline card and the DIN validation with "leave blank until NOC" hint would actually save me from silly mistakes. I think after a day of poking around I'd be fine, but the first hour would be intimidating.

Honestly this feels like a lot to take in at once. There are so many pages and cards and expanders here that I'd be nervous about clicking around on my first filing. That said, most of it seems to be read-only viewing and filtering, which is less scary than filling forms, so once someone shows me where the dossier grid and the Audit link are I think I could manage the day-to-day parts.

The three-column layout with a step rail, the active card, and a module tower on the right sounds like something I could actually follow, which is a relief because ANDS is overwhelming for me. The nav chips with tooltips and the "New to ANDS? Start here" primer feel welcoming for someone at my level. The one thing I'd worry about is that it's a lot going on at once, but it seems structured, not chaotic.

Honestly this reads like it would be pretty approachable for someone at my level. The step rail plus the "submission tower" and a readiness percentage right in the top bar means I'd always know where I am, which is more than I can say for our Word-templates-on-a-shared-drive setup. The one thing I'd worry about is the sheer number of nav areas — Journey, Dossiers, Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence — I'd need a bit of hand-holding to know which one I actually live in day to day.

Reading this, it doesn't look hard to get into — labeled fields, a disabled button until things are filled, plain-language role names instead of just codes. That's the kind of thing I appreciate, because I'm not a power user and I don't want to guess. The MFA and reset flows are described clearly enough that I could follow them without calling IT.

Honestly, the sign-in itself looks simple enough — email, password, a code from my authenticator, buttons that tell me when they're disabled and why. That part I could do. Where I'd slow down is the workspace and role setup; "CRO vs your own company," vendor roles behind expanders, security-policy toggles — I'd want to sit with someone before I touched any of that, because getting isolation wrong is a real problem in my world.

The numbered rail with a "you're here" marker and locked steps that tell me plainly why they're locked is the kind of hand-holding I'd want for the staff who actually assemble our submissions. My concern is the sheer number of moving panels — three columns, towers, expanders, toggles — which for someone at my comfort level is a lot to take in at once. I'd need to sit with it before I trusted myself to not miss something.

The numbered rail with locked steps and a plain-language reason for each lock is the kind of controlled progression I'd want, so at a basic level I could follow it. But there's a lot on one screen — three columns, a 3D tower, expanders inside expanders — and for someone who works from paper SOPs that's a fair bit to take in. The Expert mode that unlocks steps worries me more than it helps; I'd want that gated or logged.

For someone like me who lives in SOPs and Acrobat, this reads as fairly approachable — a create button, a form, filter and list views, nothing exotic. The inline validation on the Dossier ID format and the type-the-ID-plus-reason gate before archiving are the kind of friction I actually want, not obstacles. I'd want to click through it myself, but on paper I could find my way around.

Honestly this reads like something I could navigate without a two-day training course, which is more than I can say for most vault systems I sign off on. Creating a dossier is a simple inline form, and the "no ID yet, start with a placeholder" option means my team isn't blocked waiting on the Health Canada ID before they start assembling. The delete-requires-typed-ID-and-reason step is a bit of friction, but that's exactly the kind of friction I want.

Honestly this is dense. Three columns with tree badges, chips, expanders, tooltips inside tooltips - I'd need someone to walk me through it the first few times, and I don't love that. But I'll give it credit: the "Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A" choices are plain, and pre-filled known facts plus greyed "example - replace this" text would keep my people from shipping placeholder junk. Medium difficulty for someone like me.

Honestly, this is a lot to take in. Three columns, badges, chips, a dozen collapsible expanders, mode toggles inside mode toggles. I could probably learn it, but for someone like me who lives in paper SOPs and Acrobat, the first hour would be slow going, and I'd want a written procedure to lean on. That said, the fact that everything is spelled out with tooltips and teach boxes does soften the landing.

Reading it, the basic path seems manageable: pick "Author in-app," type some facts, send, review, confirm. That maps to how I already work. But there are a lot of layers stacked in one panel, expanders within expanders, two different authoring modes, toggles inside toggles, and for someone at my comfort level I'd want to be walked through it once before I trusted myself not to miss a step.

Honestly, the flow reads as manageable — three clear choices to complete a section, and the AI chat is just a box you type into. What I can't tell from a written walkthrough is how much back-and-forth the assistant demands before it gives you anything useful, and I'd want to see whether "Fill the form" is a genuine escape hatch for people like me who don't trust the chatbot. The multiple toggles-within-toggles (Author in-app, then Draft with AI vs Fill the form) is one layer more than I'd like.

Reading it, the flow seems manageable, but there's a lot going on in one card — status chips, collapsed expanders, findings toggles, parity-gap tables, a sequences panel. I'd need to sit with it and walk through it a couple of times before I trusted myself to drive it. The one thing I genuinely appreciate is that export is blocked until the check passes and the override forces you to type a reason, so it doesn't let you rush past a problem.

Honestly, this looks manageable for someone in my seat, once I got past the density. The collapsed-by-default expanders keep the screen from overwhelming me, and the override-requires-a-typed-reason step is exactly the kind of gated action I'm used to signing off on. My worry is the sheer number of chips, badges, and abbreviations packed into one card, but I wouldn't call it hard.

Honestly, this looks fairly navigable for someone in my seat — Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, and Audit are laid out the way I already think about a submission portfolio, and the scope card sitting first is sensible. My worry is the sheer density of chips, expanders, and popovers on one screen; I'd want to sit with it a while before I trusted myself not to miss something behind a collapsed "Advanced" or "Details" tab.

Honestly this reads like a lot of pages to keep straight — Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, Audit — each with its own scope card and expanders, and I'd need to be walked through it once. But the layout is sensible: summary cards up top, a grid below, details tucked behind expanders so I'm not drowning. For someone like me who signs off rather than assembles daily, I could learn it, though the acronym soup (SDN/SAL/SRL/NOD/NON, DSTS lifecycle) would slow me down at first.

Reading it, the layout sounds sensible for someone like me who signs off rather than assembles day to day, and the plain-language framing plus the readiness percentage would help me see where a submission actually stands. What I can't judge from a walkthrough is how it behaves under my hands, and that's what matters to me before I'd trust it in front of an auditor.

Reading through it, the layout sounds sensible for someone like me who reviews rather than assembles — a step rail, a readiness percentage, and a plain-language promise on every term is the kind of hand-holding my assemblers would need. I can't judge the real friction without touching it, but the guided end-to-end framing and the "type RESET to confirm" gate suggest they've thought about slips. My worry is always that "plain language" hides where the actual regulatory judgment has to happen.

Honestly this reads as easy for someone like me — the flow mirrors what I already do mentally: sign in, MFA, workspace-per-client. The CRO branch ("On behalf of clients") is exactly right for a solo practice juggling six sponsors, and disabled-until-filled buttons plus live password helper mean I wouldn't be guessing. Nothing here would make me reach for a manual.

Honestly this is about as gentle an entry as I could ask for — labeled fields, a disabled button until things are filled, Enter-to-submit, and a password rule that counts down for you. The CRO branch matters to me specifically because I file on behalf of clients, and having "On behalf of clients (CRO)" adjust the labels means I'm not fighting a form built only for single-sponsor companies. I'd have no trouble getting through sign-in, MFA, or the reset flow.

Reading it, the numbered left-hand rail with locks and plain-language reasons is the kind of scaffolding I'd want a junior at a sponsor to follow without hand-holding, so the flow itself looks manageable. My worry is the sheer density — three columns, a 3D tower, multiple expanders, a mode toggle — is a lot on screen at once, and I'd need to see whether it feels guided or cluttered in practice. The dashed-underline hover definitions for regulatory terms are a nice touch for my less-experienced clients.

The three-column layout with a numbered journey rail, an active step card, and a live readiness panel is actually how I think about a filing, so I could find my way around without much hand-holding. The step-by-step lock-and-reason approach would slow me down in places I don't need it, but the Expert mode toggle that unlocks steps as "not yet recommended" is exactly the escape hatch someone like me needs. Overall this looks straightforward to sit down with.

This reads as straightforward for someone like me who lives in this world — create a dossier, fill in ID, product, submission type, and go. The inline card with a Cancel toggle and the placeholder auto-fill is sensible. My only friction is the delete flow requiring me to type the full Dossier ID plus a reason, but honestly that friction is appropriate for a regulated file, so I don't mind it.

This reads as straightforward enough for me to navigate day one; the New dossier form asks exactly the fields I'd expect, and the filter/list-view with sort by soonest due matches how I actually juggle six or seven clients. The typed-ID-plus-reason gate on delete is a small friction, but it's the right friction, and I'd rather that than an accidental archive.

The three-column layout is dense but logically ordered, and I can see myself finding my footing quickly because it mirrors how I already think about an eCTD — module tree on the left, the leaf and its guidance in the middle, filability on the right. My worry is the sheer number of collapsed expanders; a less eCTD-literate junior at a sponsor would drown, though for me the progressive disclosure is a mercy rather than a burden.

For a regulatory hand who lives in the guidance, this is medium-easy — three columns with a section tree, a required-placed counter, and status icons is close to how my own checklists already work. My real concern is density: the right rail stacks a lot of expanders, chips, and toggles, and a junior associate at a sponsor would drown before finding the one item that's actually blocking them. I'd need to see it in motion to be sure, but on paper it suits an experienced preparer more than a novice.

Mechanically this looks straightforward — a work panel with clear toggles (Upload, Author in-app, Mark N/A), a chat box, Send, Use this draft, and a confirm button. I've never used it hands-on, but the linear flow is close to how I already move through eCTD leaves, so I wouldn't be lost. My only friction is the number of steps and expanders I'd have to click through per section, which across a full ANDS would add up.

Reading it, the path seems clear enough — pick Upload, Author in-app, or Mark N/A, then either chat with the AI or fill the form. That maps to how I actually work section by section, so I wouldn't be lost. My only friction is the number of nested disclosures and expanders; I'd be clicking around a fair bit to find the guidance and placement details I want visible at all times, not tucked behind "Format & source" and "eCTD placement."

Honestly this looks straightforward enough for me to operate — cards, chips, expanders, a findings list, and Download report buttons are all things I already navigate in eValidator and Word. The collapsed-by-default design keeps it uncluttered, though the sequences/lifecycle-operator part (new/replace chips, "working: NNNN") would take me a walkthrough or two before I'd trust myself to build a Response or Supplement sequence correctly.

For someone like me who lives in checklists and eValidator, this reads as manageable. The card-and-chip layout, the collapsed expanders, and the plain error/warning rows are familiar territory, and I'd know within a minute where to look for what failed. The only friction is the sheer number of expanders and sections, but nothing here would leave me lost.

Honestly this reads like it was built by someone who understands how we actually work, so navigating it wouldn't scare me — Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence, Audit map to real tasks I do by hand today. My worry is density: the scope card, isolation expander, litigation clocks, DSTS lifecycle and Form V register all stacked together is a lot of surface for a solo consultant to learn, and I'd need a run-through before trusting myself in it. The collapsed expanders keeping the advanced clocks out of the way is the right instinct.

Honestly this reads as manageable for someone like me who lives in this world — the Portfolio, Registry, Correspondence and Audit pages are laid out logically and the scope card sitting first is the right instinct.
